segments.chapter: Early career: New Orleans to Tulsa
segments.title: Playing on the Dewey Jackson boat band
segments.summary: Pasley recalls a book with old New Orleans musicians and says he played on a riverboat with Dewey Jackson of St. Louis, leaving New Orleans with him.

segments.chapter: Early career: New Orleans to Tulsa
segments.title: Early New Orleans bands: Peter Williams, Jack Carey, Kid Punch, Arnold DePass
segments.summary: He lists the New Orleans bandleaders he played with as a teenager, gives his 1904 birth, and names men in the Olympia band with Arnold DePass.

segments.chapter: Early career: New Orleans to Tulsa
segments.title: Leaving New Orleans with Nat Towles for Tulsa
segments.summary: Pasley left in 1924 with Towles, who recruited New Orleans players for a Tulsa band; sidemen are named and they played Oklahoma for about a year.

segments.chapter: Early career: New Orleans to Tulsa
segments.title: Travels abroad and playing with Moten and George E. Lee
segments.summary: He says he never went to Yucatan but travelled to China, the Philippines, Canada and Mexico, and briefly played with Bennie Moten and George E. Lee in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Chicago and California bands
segments.title: White Horse Tavern in Kansas City, then Chicago and California
segments.summary: He left Moten to make more money at a Kansas City tavern, then played with the Robinson Syncopators in Chicago and moved to Los Angeles, where he played in many bands.

segments.chapter: Kansas City, Chicago and California bands
segments.title: Ory band lineup, Les Hite tour east, six years with Liggins
segments.summary: With Hite from 1939 he went to New York and Boston until wartime, then spent about six years with Joe Liggins; he now plays only occasional gigs.

segments.title: Starting on piano, banjo and playing in bands
segments.summary: Asked about piano, he says he started on it, read music for Dixieland bands, played for money on banjo from youth, and never played solo alone.

segments.title: Recording with Joe Liggins and the band personnel
segments.summary: He made all of Liggins's records and lists the six men who played on them.

segments.title: First recording, Chicago 1925, with Richard M. Jones
segments.summary: His first date was a 1925 pickup session for OKeh led by pianist Richard M. Jones, with Preston Jackson, Omer Simeon and Jabbo Smith; he cannot recall titles.

segments.title: Records with Leon Rene in Los Angeles
segments.summary: He recorded in the early 1930s with Leon Rene's small band, naming sidemen, and says most of his work was in big bands before Liggins.

segments.title: Session and studio work, including Wynonie Harris
segments.summary: He made over a hundred sessions in blues and rhythm groups, including Wynonie Harris, and earned the most money in studios.

segments.title: Learning banjo in New Orleans from the Hanley brothers
segments.summary: He started on ukulele then banjo with German teachers at Werlein's music store, took lessons from Dewey White, and later learned guitar in California.

segments.title: Guitar sessions with Danny Barker, Irving Ashby and Oscar Moore
segments.summary: He says he learned guitar by trading ideas with other guitarists in sessions at his house.

segments.title: Barrelhouse pianists he knew in New Orleans
segments.summary: After a remark about Little Brother Montgomery, he names Jelly Roll Morton, Walter Pichon and Joe Robichaux as pianists he knew.

segments.title: Udell Wilson and Willie Jackson at the Lyric Theater
segments.summary: He recalls pianist Udell Wilson playing a cabaret with singer Willie Jackson near the Lyric Theater, and Charlie Love and other trumpeters.

segments.title: Blues singers visiting New Orleans: Bessie Smith, Clara Smith, Ida Cox
segments.summary: He remembers seeing Bessie Smith's first visit and other blues singers, and mentions Louis Armstrong and Zutty Singleton.

segments.title: Red Caillou and his move to California
segments.summary: Pasley describes his boyhood friend Red Caillou, who moved to California about 1925 and died in Oakland.

segments.title: Growing up with Alvin Alcorn
segments.summary: He says he and Alvin Alcorn were raised together, and shows the interviewer a picture.

segments.title: Alcorn's cousin George McCullum and a Chicago musician address
segments.summary: They discuss whether McCullum and Alcorn were cousins, Clarence Desdunes's band, and a Jimmy Gordon combo in Chicago.

segments.title: His cousin pianist Adam Cato
segments.summary: Pasley says Adam Cato of San Diego is his cousin, a versatile pianist who made many records, and the interviewer asks where to find him.

segments.title: When Adam Cato moved to California
segments.summary: Cato moved west for good in 1948 around the time of Pasley's father's death; Pasley himself came in 1926.

segments.title: Uncle Tapp Cato and Adam Cato Sr., drummer
segments.summary: He names his pianist uncle Tapp and Adam's drummer father, who played parades.

segments.title: Trying to find Adam Cato's address
segments.summary: The group tries to find Cato's address in the book and phone directory.

segments.title: Straightening out the Cato family tree
segments.summary: The interviewer sorts out the Catos; Pasley adds his aunts who played piano after Catholic school training.

segments.title: Writing down addresses, Al Morgan and Dauphine Street
segments.summary: Addresses are exchanged amid noise; Pasley says he is leaving town the next night.

segments.title: Fred Washington, pianist who could read music
segments.summary: Pasley worked with Fred Washington at a taxi dancehall; they compare his reading ability with Jelly Roll Morton's.

segments.title: Dink Johnson, George Baquet and Jimmy Palao in California
segments.summary: They discuss Dink Johnson, who came west with King Oliver's band, and others playing in Los Angeles before 1917.

segments.title: Addresses and finding Alvin Pernell
segments.summary: Dolphin Street address and telephone are given and Pasley points the interviewer to Alton Purnell.

segments.title: Alton Purnell's band and Joe Darensbourg
segments.summary: He names members of Purnell's current band and says he played with Joe Darensbourg a long time.

segments.title: Pencil and paper; Kid Punch still living
segments.summary: Writing materials; interviewer comments on many New Orleans musicians still in California.

segments.title: Burns session opens: a barrelhouse piano man
segments.summary: Buddy Burns, in a separate session, tries to recall a barrelhouse pianist and prepares to play.

segments.title: Salty Dog blues, Sonny Swan and Papa Charlie Jackson
segments.summary: Burns says he played this tune from age eight and learned it from Sonny Swan in the district; Papa Charlie Jackson recorded it later.

segments.title: Buster Anderson and Bert Russell's dirty blues
segments.summary: Burns and his wife recall pianist Buster Anderson who played blues with Bert Russell.

segments.title: John Slingsby's recordings and Burns's waltz
segments.summary: The interviewer mentions Slingsby taping Burns; Burns says Warren and Jim Fisher played his waltz differently.

segments.title: Naming the Dirty Dozens blues
segments.summary: Burns says his blues was nameless but kids called it the Dirty Dozens.

segments.title: Ernest O'Cos, barrelhouse pianist
segments.summary: Burns describes O'Cos, who worked in France, played barrelhouse, and died decades earlier.

segments.title: Alex, the one-legged piano player
segments.summary: They try to recall the real name of an older one-legged district pianist.

segments.title: Robert Boynes and playing fish fries and the district
segments.summary: Burns's younger brother Robert played bell house piano; Burns played fish fries and sometimes the district.

segments.title: Sam Morgan, Jack Carey and Buddy Petit bands
segments.summary: Burns recalls rival bands at a club and who played trumpet with Carey and Petit.

segments.title: George Washington and George Orendorff
segments.summary: A muddle about which George played trombone on a picture; Orendorff is a trumpeter still living.

segments.title: Everett Swan, Burns's valet
segments.summary: Sonny Swan's real name was Everett; he drove for Burns and watched his money when Burns ran gambling clubs.

segments.title: Brothers Tom and Robert Boynes
segments.summary: Burns names brother Tom (James) Boynes, a piano player in New Orleans, and dead brother Robert.

segments.title: A family of pianists and musicians
segments.summary: Burns's sister, children and grandsons played music.

segments.title: Walter Hall and other musicians
segments.summary: They discuss whether Walter Hall was a pianist or drummer; transcript degrades into loops.

segments.title: Drive 'Em Down and Son Miller
segments.summary: Burns explains that Son Miller played the blues Drive 'Em Down and was older than he.

segments.title: Son Godet and Son Miller
segments.summary: Burns mentions Son Godet, who played piano and trumpet, and Miller's early blues.

segments.title: Buttsy Miller, his brother, and his decline
segments.summary: They discuss William Miller called Buttsy; Burns's brother Tom says he lost his mind through drink.
